summary:
The "Police Our Border Act" (H.R. 8146, 118th Congress) is a single-purpose reporting bill directing the Attorney General to submit one report to Congress concerning the asserted impact of border conditions on Federal, State, local, and Tribal law enforcement. As passed by the House on May 16, 2024, and received in the Senate and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on May 20, 2024, the bill contains no amendments to existing statute, no appropriation, and no authorization of appropriations.

Section 1 provides the short title. Section 2 sets forth congressional findings, including references to line-of-duty officer deaths reported by the National Law Enforcement Officer Memorial Fund, characterizations of the "Biden border crisis," and a statement that it is in the interest of law enforcement for Congress to enact border security legislation and for the President to utilize existing authorities, "including under section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1182(f))." These findings are hortatory and impose no operative legal obligation; the reference to INA § 212(f) is descriptive and does not amend or invoke that authority.

Section 3 is the sole operative provision. It requires the Attorney General, "not later than 180 days after the date of enactment," to submit to Congress a report on the impact the border situation is having on law enforcement officers at all four governmental levels. The report must address seven enumerated matters: (1) the estimated dollar value of all resources devoted to addressing the border crisis and the extent to which those resources are diverted from law enforcement agencies; (2) officer exposure to fentanyl arising from encounters with "illegal aliens" at the border and within the United States, including the nationality of each such alien; (3) officer injuries connected to the border crisis or fentanyl exposure; (4) officer morale; (5) the effect on law enforcement recruiting and hiring; (6) estimated State expenditures on local law enforcement efforts to investigate, intercept, and process trafficked fentanyl, encompassing the entire evidence lifecycle from collection and analysis through storage and destruction; and (7) the number of officers reassigned and local resources reallocated for such fentanyl-related activities across the same evidence lifecycle.

The bill establishes no enforcement mechanism, funding, penalty, or ongoing reporting requirement beyond the single 180-day deliverable, and specifies no effective date other than that keyed to enactment.
